Lesson 01: Web Technologies for Roboticists — HTTP, Methods & JSON

Welcome to Level 2 of the NavPro Robotics Workshop! In Level 1, you mastered the real-time robotics fundamentals: ROS 2 nodes, topics, services, actions, TF2 coordinate transforms, Gazebo physics simulation, and Nav2 autonomous navigation.

However, in commercial robotics systems (such as warehouse AMRs, hospital delivery fleets, and autonomous inspection rovers), robots must communicate with the outside world: web browsers, mobile apps, enterprise ERP systems, and cloud fleet servers.

In this lesson, you will master the foundational language of the modern web: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), request methods, status codes, and JSON serialization for robotics.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the Client-Server model and how it contrasts with ROS 2 peer-to-peer DDS pub/sub.
  2. Dissect an HTTP packet: Request Line, Headers, Query Parameters, and Body.
  3. Apply standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to physical robotics operations.
  4. Interpret and use industrial HTTP status codes (200 OK, 202 Accepted, 400, 422, 500).
  5. Serialize complex ROS 2 telemetry objects into standard JSON payloads.

2. The Client-Server Model vs. ROS 2 DDS

In ROS 2, nodes use DDS (Data Distribution Service) over UDP multicast. Every node discovers every other node dynamically as peers.

In the web ecosystem, the world operates on the Client-Server Architecture:

BASH
      ROS 2 DDS (Peer-to-Peer Multicast):
      [ Node A ] <─── UDP Multicast ───> [ Node B ]
          │                                  │
          └─────────── [ Node C ] ───────────┘

      Web / Enterprise Cloud (Client-Server):
      [ Web Browser / Cockpit ]  ─── Request (TCP) ───>  [ Robot Gateway Server ]
                                 <─── Response (JSON) ──
  • Client: The initiator of the communication (e.g. a web browser dashboard, mobile app, or Python script).
  • Server: The robot's onboard API gateway daemon listening on a dedicated port (e.g. port 8080 or 8090).
  • Statelessness: By default, each HTTP transaction is independent. The server processes the request and closes or reuses the TCP connection.

3. Dissecting an HTTP Request & Response

When a web browser clicks a button to inspect a robot, it transmits an HTTP request over TCP:

3.1 Raw HTTP Request Packet

HTTP
POST /api/v1/navigation/goal HTTP/1.1
Host: 192.168.1.100:8080
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer navpro_operator_token_456
User-Agent: NavPro-Cockpit/2.0

{
  "x": 4.5,
  "y": 2.0,
  "yaw": 1.57
}
  • Request Line: POST /api/v1/navigation/goal HTTP/1.1 specifies the method, resource path, and HTTP version.
  • Headers: Metadata key-value pairs (Content-Type: application/json tells the server the body is JSON).
  • Body: The payload carrying our target $(x, y, \theta)$ coordinates.

3.2 Raw HTTP Response Packet

HTTP
HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Content-Type: application/json
Date: Tue, 13 Oct 2026 12:00:00 GMT

{
  "status": "ACCEPTED",
  "goal_id": "nav_88a91b",
  "message": "Navigation goal accepted and dispatched to Nav2."
}

4. HTTP Methods Mapped to Robotics Operations

In RESTful robotics design, we map standard HTTP verbs to specific robot actions:

HTTP Method Purpose in Robotics Example Robotics Endpoint Expected Payload
GET Read-Only State: Safe and idempotent. Never triggers physical motion. GET /api/v1/telemetry<br>GET /api/v1/battery None (reads cached state).
POST Action Trigger: Dispatches actuation, creates new goals, triggers E-Stop. POST /api/v1/navigation/goal<br>POST /api/v1/emergency_stop JSON containing parameters: {"x": 2.5, "y": 1.0}.
PUT / PATCH State Update: Modifies stored configuration or existing landmark. PUT /api/v1/waypoints/station_a JSON: {"x": 3.0, "y": 1.5}.
DELETE Cancellation / Deletion: Cancels an active goal or removes a waypoint. DELETE /api/v1/navigation/active_goal<br>DELETE /api/v1/waypoints/old_dock None or cancellation reason.
Safety Rule: GET Requests Must Never Move the Robot!
Web browsers, search indexers, and proxies frequently pre-fetch GET URLs automatically. If you configure GET /api/v1/move_forward to publish velocity to /cmd_vel, your robot could drive into a wall simply because someone opened a browser bookmark! Always use POST for physical actuation.

5. Industrial HTTP Status Codes for Autonomous Fleets

When the robot responds to a client, the status code communicates what happened:

BASH
        HTTP Status Code Families:
        ├── 2xx (Success): Request received, understood, and accepted.
        ├── 4xx (Client Error): Client sent invalid data, missing auth, or illegal values.
        └── 5xx (Server Error): Robot backend crashed or ROS 2 node died.
Status Code Name Practical Robotics Meaning
200 OK Standard Success Telemetry read succeeded, or parameter was updated successfully.
202 Accepted Asynchronous Job Queued Critical for Nav2 actions! Tells client: "We validated your goal and dispatched it to the robot. Motion has begun in the background."
400 Bad Request Malformed Syntax JSON syntax error or missing mandatory fields.
401 Unauthorized Missing Authentication No API token or Bearer key supplied.
403 Forbidden Insufficient Role User is a Viewer attempting to trigger Admin manual teleop.
404 Not Found Missing Resource Requested landmark name or goal_id does not exist in memory.
409 Conflict State Conflict Request cannot execute due to robot state (e.g. attempting to navigate while Emergency Stop is ENGAGED).
422 Unprocessable Entity Pydantic Validation Error Coordinate exceeds allowable warehouse bounds or velocity is NaN.
500 Internal Error Hardware/Software Fault Motor driver disconnected, ROS 2 executor exception, or lidar crash.

6. JSON Data Encoding for Robotics

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the universal data format of the web. Here is how ROS 2 message types map into clean JSON:

PYTHON
import json
import time

# Converting ROS 2 Odometry & Battery into Web JSON
telemetry_data = {
    "robot_id": "navpro-mini-amr",
    "timestamp": time.time(),
    "pose": {
        "x": 4.25,      # meters
        "y": 1.50,      # meters
        "yaw": 1.57     # radians
    },
    "velocity": {
        "linear": 0.45,  # m/s
        "angular": 0.05  # rad/s
    },
    "battery": {
        "percentage": 88.5,
        "is_charging": False,
        "voltage": 24.2
    },
    "status": "NAVIGATING"
}

# Serialize to string
json_payload = json.dumps(telemetry_data)
print("Serialized JSON Size:", len(json_payload), "bytes")

7. Summary & Next Steps

In this lesson, you mastered the core web fundamentals:

  • The Client-Server model establishes a clean boundary between external clients and onboard robot software.
  • Standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) map cleanly to queries vs. physical actuation.
  • HTTP status codes (200, 202, 409, 422) communicate success and failure states deterministically.

In Lesson 02, we will examine WebSockets vs. HTTP Polling: discovering how persistent full-duplex sockets eliminate bandwidth waste for high-speed $20\,\text{Hz}$ telemetry streaming!

lessons.html_content:
Lesson 02: Real-Time WebSockets vs. HTTP Polling

In Lesson 01, we learned how the HTTP request-response cycle works for discrete operations like requesting status or dispatching a goal.

However, an Autonomous Mobile Robot is a dynamic, continuous physical system. Its wheels rotate at $50\,\text{Hz}$, odometry updates at $20\,\text{Hz}$, and LiDAR scans arrive at $10\,\text{Hz}$. When a remote operator watches the robot navigate on a map canvas, they need smooth, real-time telemetry updates.

In this lesson, you will learn why HTTP Polling fails for high-frequency robotics streaming and master Real-Time WebSockets.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the latency, bandwidth, and connection exhaustion bottlenecks of HTTP polling.
  2. Master the WebSocket Protocol (RFC 6455) lifecycle from HTTP handshake to full-duplex pipe.
  3. Understand WebSocket framing: Text vs. Binary opcodes, ping/pong heartbeats, and close frames.
  4. Compare network overhead between polling and WebSockets with mathematical proofs.
  5. Implement a minimal Python WebSocket client and server connection.

2. The Bottleneck: Why HTTP Polling Fails for Robotics

When beginners want live robot updates, they typically write a frontend timer that polls the robot repeatedly:

JAVASCRIPT
// ❌ NAIVE HTTP POLLING (20 times per second)
setInterval(async () => {
    const res = await fetch("http://192.168.1.100:8080/api/v1/telemetry");
    const data = await res.json();
    updateMap(data.x, data.y);
}, 50); // 50ms = 20Hz
BASH
HTTP Polling (20 requests every second):
Client ──[SYN/ACK TCP]──> Server ──[TLS Handshake]──> Server
Client ──[GET Request (850B headers)]──> Server
Server ──[HTTP 200 OK (300B headers + 120B payload)]──> Client
Client ──[FIN/ACK Close]──> Server
(Repeat this entire cycle 20 times every single second!)

Three Devastating Consequences:

  1. Header Bloat: Every HTTP/1.1 request sends $\approx 850\,\text{bytes}$ of redundant headers (User-Agent, Host, Cookie, Accept, Keep-Alive) just to transfer $120\,\text{bytes}$ of coordinate numbers ($88\%$ bandwidth waste!).
  2. TCP Socket Exhaustion: Rapidly opening and closing TCP connections leaves hundreds of sockets in the TIME_WAIT state on the robot's Linux kernel, eventually exhausting ephemeral ports (Errno 99: Cannot assign requested address).
  3. Head-of-Line Latency Jitter: If one HTTP request experiences a Wi-Fi packet drop, subsequent requests queue up, resulting in stuttering, laggy map visualization.

3. The Modern Solution: The WebSocket Protocol

WebSocket (RFC 6455) establishes a persistent, bi-directional, full-duplex TCP connection between client and robot over a single socket.

MERMAID
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as Browser / Cockpit
    participant Gateway as Robot WebSocket Server

    Note over Client,Gateway: 1. HTTP Upgrade Handshake
    Client->>Gateway: GET /ws/telemetry HTTP/1.1<br/>Upgrade: websocket<br/>Connection: Upgrade<br/>Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
    Gateway-->>Client: HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols<br/>Upgrade: websocket<br/>Connection: Upgrade<br/>Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

    Note over Client,Gateway: 2. Full-Duplex Streaming Pipe (Zero HTTP Headers!)
    loop 20 times every second (20Hz)
        Gateway->>Client: Frame: {"x": 1.25, "y": 3.40, "yaw": 0.12, "battery": 88.5} (Only 2 bytes frame overhead!)
    end

    Note over Client,Gateway: 3. Bi-Directional Ping / Pong Heartbeats
    Client->>Gateway: Opcode 0x9 (PING)
    Gateway-->>Client: Opcode 0xA (PONG)

4. Mathematical Comparison: Polling vs. WebSockets

Let us calculate the bandwidth consumed by 1 operator dashboard streaming robot pose at $20\,\text{Hz}$ over a $1\text{-hour}$ mission:

$$\text{Total Packets in 1 Hour} = 20\,\text{Hz} \times 3600\,\text{s} = 72{,}000\,\text{packets}$$

Case A: HTTP Polling (20Hz)

$$\text{Per-Request Overhead} \approx 850\,\text{B (Req)} + 300\,\text{B (Resp Headers)} + 120\,\text{B (Payload)} = 1{,}270\,\text{bytes}$$

$$\text{Total Data Transferred} = 72{,}000 \times 1{,}270\,\text{B} = 91{,}440{,}000\,\text{bytes} \approx \mathbf{91.4\,\text{MB / hour}}$$

Case B: WebSocket Stream (20Hz)

$$\text{Handshake Overhead} \approx 1{,}200\,\text{bytes (one-time only)}$$

$$\text{Per-Frame Overhead} = 2\,\text{bytes (Frame Header)} + 120\,\text{bytes (JSON Payload)} = 122\,\text{bytes}$$

$$\text{Total Data Transferred} = 1{,}200 + (72{,}000 \times 122\,\text{B}) = 8{,}785{,}200\,\text{bytes} \approx \mathbf{8.8\,\text{MB / hour}}$$

Performance Gain:
Switching from HTTP polling to WebSockets reduces network bandwidth by over $90\%$, lowers latency from $\approx 45\,\text{ms}$ to $<5\,\text{ms}$, and completely prevents socket exhaustion on onboard robot computers!

5. WebSocket Framing & Opcode Specifications

Inside the TCP stream, WebSockets transmits discrete binary frames:

Opcode (Hex) Frame Type Meaning in Robotics
0x1 Text Frame UTF-8 encoded string (typically JSON telemetry: pose, battery, states).
0x2 Binary Frame Raw binary payload (used for compressed JPEG camera frames or occupancy grid arrays).
0x8 Connection Close Graceful shutdown handshake initiated by either client or robot.
0x9 Ping Heartbeat probe sent by client or server to check network liveness.
0xA Pong Unsolicited or solicited heartbeat reply verifying active connection.

6. Summary & Next Steps

In this lesson, you analyzed real-time communication protocols:

  • Demonstrated why HTTP polling causes severe bandwidth bloat and socket exhaustion.
  • Mastered the WebSocket protocol lifecycle and framing mechanisms.
  • Proved mathematically that WebSockets deliver a $90\%$ bandwidth reduction with sub-$5\text{ms}$ latencies.

In Lesson 03, we will study The Dual-Plane Architecture: designing the boundary between this web layer and the real-time ROS 2 control plane!

WebSockets establish a single persistent TCP connection with only 2 to 6 bytes of framing overhead per message, avoiding repeated HTTP handshake latency and header bloat
HTTP polling cannot transmit JSON data
WebSockets bypass Linux network permissions
quizzes.explanation: HTTP polling sends ~800 bytes of headers on every single request and introduces TCP connection overhead. WebSockets maintain a full-duplex socket with microsecond latency and tiny 2-byte frame headers.

Lesson 03: Enterprise System Architecture — The Dual-Plane Model

In Lessons 01 and 02, we established the communication foundations: HTTP for discrete transactional commands and WebSockets for high-frequency streaming.

Now, we address the architectural question that defines commercial robotics engineering: Where does the web layer meet the robot's real-time controllers?

In this lesson, you will learn the Dual-Plane Architecture, the industry-standard design pattern deployed in commercial fleets (including Amazon Robotics, OTTO Motors, and the NavPro Mini Platform).

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Identify the architectural responsibilities of the Real-Time Control Plane vs. the Application / Cloud Plane.
  2. Explain why exposing raw DDS sockets to web frontends violates safety and scalability principles.
  3. Design the High-Performance Bridge Layer with thread isolation and mutex-protected memory caching.
  4. Calculate end-to-end latency budgets from wheel encoder ticks to web browser canvas pixels.
  5. Contrast custom API gateways with generic bridges like rosbridge_suite.

2. The Dual-Plane Architectural Blueprint

To guarantee robot safety and high web responsiveness, we divide the software stack into two isolated execution planes:

MERMAID
graph TB
    subgraph App_Plane["Application / Cloud Plane (Non-Real-Time, High Concurrency)"]
        Browser["Fleet Cockpit Web UI"]
        Mobile["Operator Smartwatch Badge"]
        ERP["Warehouse Management System (WMS)"]
        LLM["AI Agent (Claude / Gemini via MCP)"]
    end

    subgraph Bridge_Layer["High-Performance Asynchronous Bridge Layer"]
        FastAPI["FastAPI ASGI REST Gateway (:8080)"]
        WS_Server["20Hz Telemetry WebSocket Broadcaster"]
        State_Cache[("Thread-Safe Telemetry Cache & Mutex")]
        Action_Queue["Non-Blocking Nav2 Dispatch Queue"]
    end

    subgraph Control_Plane["Real-Time Control Plane (ROS 2 Jazzy, Hard/Soft RT)"]
        Executor["rclpy MultiThreadedExecutor Daemon"]
        Nav2["Nav2 Simple Commander & Path Planner"]
        Odom["Wheel Encoders & IMU EKF Node"]
        Safety["Laser Arbiter & Hardware E-Stop Supervisor"]
        Drivers["Differential Drive Motor Actuators"]
    end

    Browser <-->|HTTP REST / 20Hz WS| FastAPI
    Mobile <-->|HTTP / Lightweight WS| FastAPI
    ERP <-->|REST Webhooks| FastAPI
    LLM <-->|Model Context Protocol| FastAPI

    FastAPI <-->|Atomic Reads/Writes| State_Cache
    WS_Server <-->|20Hz Snapshots| State_Cache
    FastAPI -->|Async Job Tokens| Action_Queue

    Action_Queue -->|ROS 2 Action Clients| Executor
    Executor -->|rclpy Subscriptions| State_Cache

    Executor <--> Nav2
    Executor <--> Odom
    Executor <--> Safety
    Safety <--> Drivers

3. Comparing the Execution Planes

Dimension Real-Time Control Plane (ROS 2) Application & Cloud Plane (Web Gateway)
Primary Goal Determinism & Safety: Motors must stop if obstacles appear within $50\,\text{ms}$. Concurrency & Usability: Handle multiple web clients, auth, and remote commands.
Transport DDS UDP Multicast on ROS_DOMAIN_ID. HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, WebSockets over TCP on port 8080.
Latency Bounds Hard/Soft Real-Time ($<10\,\text{ms}$ bounded jitter). Best-effort network latency ($10 - 200\,\text{ms}$).
Fault Recovery Fail-safe: halt motors immediately if heartbeat drops. Graceful degradation: reconnect, retry with exponential backoff.
Threading OS threads pinned to CPU cores, high-priority executors. Asynchronous event loop (asyncio, uvloop, ASGI).

4. Why Generic Direct Bridges (rosbridge_suite) Fail in Production

Many academic projects rely on rosbridge_suite to connect web browsers to ROS 2. While suitable for quick lab tests, it creates severe vulnerabilities in commercial production:

  1. Schema Coupling: Exposes raw ROS 2 message definitions (geometry_msgs/msg/TwistStamped) to frontend JavaScript. If you modify a ROS package, all frontend dashboards break!
  2. Security Vulnerability: Any browser client with a WebSocket connection can publish directly to sensitive internal topics (like /motor_raw_pwm or /reset_odom).
  3. Bandwidth Explosion: Transmitting raw point clouds or uncompressed laser scans over web sockets saturates Wi-Fi networks immediately.
  4. No Business Validation: Cannot enforce coordinate bounds, rate limits, or user authorization tokens.

By designing our own FastAPI & WebSocket Gateway, we enforce clean API schemas, user authentication, and physical safety constraints!

5. End-to-End Latency Budget

Let us trace the time required for a wheel rotation to appear on the operator's web screen:

BASH
[Wheel Tick] ──1ms──> [ESP32 Micro-ROS] ──2ms──> [ROS 2 /odom Ingestion]
     ──0.1ms──> [Thread-Safe Cache Write] ──12ms (avg wait in 20Hz loop)──> 
     [WebSocket Broadcast] ──4ms (Local Wi-Fi)──> [Browser Render]
     ==============================================================
     TOTAL END-TO-END LATENCY: < 20 ms (Smooth 50-60 FPS UI experience!)

6. Summary & Next Steps

In this lesson, you mastered system architecture:

  • Segregated software into the Real-Time Control Plane and Application Plane.
  • Understood why generic direct DDS bridges fail in commercial deployments.
  • Analyzed the end-to-end latency pipeline guaranteeing sub-$20\text{ms}$ telepresence.

In Lesson 04, we will implement the engine driving this bridge: High-Concurrency ROS 2 Execution with MultiThreadedExecutor & Thread-Safe Caches!

lessons.html_content:
Lesson 04: High-Concurrency ROS 2 Execution — MultiThreadedExecutor & Mutex Caches

In Lesson 03, we designed the Dual-Plane Architecture. To make this architecture function in code, we must solve a major concurrency problem in rclpy.

By default, ROS 2 Python nodes process callbacks sequentially on a single thread. When multiple high-frequency topics, services, and web bridge queries arrive simultaneously, a single-threaded executor causes starvation and severe latency spikes.

In this lesson, you will learn how to configure the MultiThreadedExecutor, manage callback groups, and implement thread-safe state sharing in Python.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the architectural limitations of the default SingleThreadedExecutor.
  2. Configure and deploy the rclpy.executors.MultiThreadedExecutor with managed worker thread pools.
  3. Differentiate between MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup and ReentrantCallbackGroup.
  4. Use Python threading.Lock to guarantee atomic state sharing between ROS 2 subscriber callbacks and web API endpoints.
  5. Prevent common concurrency pitfalls: deadlocks, race conditions, and priority inversion.

2. SingleThreadedExecutor vs. MultiThreadedExecutor

When you run standard ROS 2 code using rclpy.spin(node), ROS 2 uses a SingleThreadedExecutor:

BASH
SingleThreadedExecutor (Sequential FIFO Queue):
[ /odom callback ] ──> [ /scan callback ] ──> [ Long Service Call (Blocks 2s) ] ──> [ /battery STALLED! ]

If any callback performs a blocking operation (such as waiting for a service response, disk I/O, or mathematical calculations), every other subscriber, timer, and action feedback callback is completely blocked. For an AMR driving at $1.5\,\text{m/s}$, a $500\,\text{ms}$ delay in processing laser scans or odometry can lead to collision!

The MultiThreadedExecutor

The MultiThreadedExecutor allocates a pool of worker OS threads (defaulting to the number of CPU cores). When an event occurs (a topic message arrives or a timer triggers), the executor assigns that callback to the next available worker thread:

MERMAID
graph TD
    Queue["DDS Event Notification Queue"]
    Exec["MultiThreadedExecutor (Thread Pool)"]
    T1["Worker Thread 1: /odom (50Hz)"]
    T2["Worker Thread 2: /scan (10Hz)"]
    T3["Worker Thread 3: Long-running Action Client"]
    T4["Worker Thread 4: Web Bridge State Read"]

    Queue --> Exec
    Exec --> T1
    Exec --> T2
    Exec --> T3
    Exec --> T4

3. Callback Groups in ROS 2

Even with a MultiThreadedExecutor, ROS 2 enforces safety rules regarding which callbacks can execute concurrently. This is governed by Callback Groups:

3.1 MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup (Default)

  • Rule: Only one callback belonging to this group can execute at any given time.
  • Use Case: Operations that mutate non-thread-safe internal state (e.g. updating a PID controller's integral accumulator).
  • Caveat: If a timer in this group calls a ROS 2 service whose response callback is in the same group, your node will deadlock permanently!

3.2 ReentrantCallbackGroup

  • Rule: Callbacks in this group can execute concurrently across multiple threads. Multiple instances of the same callback or different callbacks can run at the exact same moment.
  • Use Case: High-throughput telemetry subscribers, web bridge read handlers, and non-blocking service clients.
  • Requirement: You must protect all shared mutable variables with explicit thread synchronization locks (threading.Lock).
PYTHON
from rclpy.callback_groups import MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup, ReentrantCallbackGroup

class DualPlaneBridgeNode(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('dual_plane_bridge_node')
        
        # Group for high-frequency concurrent sensor streams
        self.sensor_cb_group = ReentrantCallbackGroup()
        
        # Group for delicate actuator control commands
        self.motor_cb_group = MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup()

4. Thread-Safe State Sharing with threading.Lock

In Python, the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) does not protect your application from race conditions when modifying complex data structures like dictionaries or object attributes across multiple threads.

To share telemetry between ROS 2 subscriber callbacks and the web API, we encapsulate shared state inside a thread-safe container using threading.Lock:

PYTHON
import threading
from typing import Dict, Any

class ThreadSafeRobotState:
    """Thread-safe cache storing latest robot telemetry."""
    
    def __init__(self):
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._data = {
            "x": 0.0,
            "y": 0.0,
            "yaw": 0.0,
            "linear_velocity": 0.0,
            "angular_velocity": 0.0,
            "battery_percentage": 100.0,
            "emergency_stop": False,
            "timestamp": 0.0
        }

    def update_pose_and_velocity(self, x: float, y: float, yaw: float, v: float, w: float):
        """Called by high-frequency ROS 2 /odom subscriber callback."""
        with self._lock:
            self._data["x"] = x
            self._data["y"] = y
            self._data["yaw"] = yaw
            self._data["linear_velocity"] = v
            self._data["angular_velocity"] = w

    def update_battery(self, percentage: float):
        """Called by /battery_state subscriber callback."""
        with self._lock:
            self._data["battery_percentage"] = percentage

    def get_snapshot(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Called by FastAPI REST / WebSocket threads to serialize state."""
        with self._lock:
            # Return a shallow copy so reading threads never mutate the active cache
            return self._data.copy()

5. Complete Implementation: MultiThreaded Background Worker

Here is the complete reference implementation showing how to launch MultiThreadedExecutor inside an isolated Python background thread:

PYTHON
import threading
import time
import math
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.executors import MultiThreadedExecutor
from rclpy.callback_groups import ReentrantCallbackGroup
from nav_msgs.msg import Odometry
from sensor_msgs.msg import BatteryState

class TelemetryCollectorNode(Node):
    def __init__(self, state_cache: ThreadSafeRobotState):
        super().__init__('telemetry_collector_node')
        self.state_cache = state_cache
        self.reentrant_group = ReentrantCallbackGroup()

        # Ingest odometry at 20-50Hz
        self.odom_sub = self.create_subscription(
            Odometry,
            '/odom',
            self.odom_callback,
            10,
            callback_group=self.reentrant_group
        )

        # Ingest battery state at 1Hz
        self.battery_sub = self.create_subscription(
            BatteryState,
            '/battery_state',
            self.battery_callback,
            10,
            callback_group=self.reentrant_group
        )
        self.get_logger().info("TelemetryCollectorNode initialized with MultiThreadedExecutor.")

    def odom_callback(self, msg: Odometry):
        x = msg.pose.pose.position.x
        y = msg.pose.pose.position.y
        
        # Quaternion to Yaw calculation
        q = msg.pose.pose.orientation
        siny_cosp = 2.0 * (q.w * q.z + q.x * q.y)
        cosy_cosp = 1.0 - 2.0 * (q.y * q.y + q.z * q.z)
        yaw = math.atan2(siny_cosp, cosy_cosp)
        
        lin_v = msg.twist.twist.linear.x
        ang_w = msg.twist.twist.angular.z

        self.state_cache.update_pose_and_velocity(x, y, yaw, lin_v, ang_w)

    def battery_callback(self, msg: BatteryState):
        pct = msg.percentage * 100.0 if msg.percentage <= 1.0 else msg.percentage
        self.state_cache.update_battery(pct)


def start_ros2_background_daemon(state_cache: ThreadSafeRobotState) -> threading.Thread:
    """Spawns rclpy MultiThreadedExecutor in an isolated OS daemon thread."""
    def worker():
        rclpy.init()
        node = TelemetryCollectorNode(state_cache)
        executor = MultiThreadedExecutor(num_threads=4)
        executor.add_node(node)
        try:
            executor.spin()
        finally:
            node.destroy_node()
            rclpy.shutdown()

    t = threading.Thread(target=worker, daemon=True, name="ROS2-Executor-Worker")
    t.start()
    return t

6. Summary & Next Steps

In this lesson, you mastered concurrent ROS 2 execution:

  • Deployed the MultiThreadedExecutor to eliminate single-threaded callback starvation.
  • Used ReentrantCallbackGroup for concurrent sensor ingestion.
  • Implemented threading.Lock mutexes to guarantee thread-safe cache updates.

In Lesson 05, we will connect this thread-safe state cache to FastAPI, creating our production REST endpoints and Pydantic validation schemas!

Lesson 05: Building the Robot REST API Gateway with FastAPI

In Lesson 04, we implemented the thread-safe MultiThreadedExecutor background worker. Now, we will wrap this worker inside FastAPI, building our production REST API Gateway.

FastAPI is the industry standard for high-performance Python microservices. Built on the Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface (ASGI), it provides asynchronous non-blocking request handling, automated Pydantic v2 validation, and auto-generated Swagger documentation.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Embed the rclpy background daemon into FastAPI using modern @asynccontextmanager lifespans.
  2. Define Pydantic v2 data models that enforce physical velocity limits ($[-1.0, 1.0]\,\text{m/s}$) and coordinate bounds.
  3. Construct core REST endpoints: GET /api/v1/system/health, GET /api/v1/telemetry, POST /api/v1/teleop, and POST /api/v1/emergency_stop.
  4. Automatically generate interactive OpenAPI (Swagger) documentation at /docs.
  5. Test endpoints using curl and verify automated HTTP 422 input rejection.

2. Lifespan Management: Starting & Stopping ROS 2 in FastAPI

In modern FastAPI, the @asynccontextmanager lifespan pattern manages external background services during server startup and shutdown:

PYTHON
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI
import rclpy

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Startup: Initialize ROS 2 and spawn background worker
    print("[FastAPI Lifespan] Initializing ROS 2 Jazzy subsystem...")
    rclpy.init()
    # (Launch background MultiThreadedExecutor thread here...)
    yield
    # Shutdown: Halt robot and teardown cleanly
    print("[FastAPI Lifespan] Shutting down ROS 2 subsystems cleanly...")
    if rclpy.ok():
        rclpy.shutdown()

app = FastAPI(
    title="NavPro Robot API Gateway",
    version="2.0.0",
    lifespan=lifespan
)

3. Pydantic v2 Robotics Data Models

Pydantic v2 enforces physical safety constraints before any command reaches the ROS 2 /cmd_vel publisher:

PYTHON
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator
from typing import Dict, Any
import math

class TeleopPayload(BaseModel):
    """Payload for manual velocity commands."""
    linear_x: float = Field(
        ...,
        ge=-1.0,
        le=1.0,
        description="Forward/reverse velocity setpoint (m/s). Clamped between -1.0 and +1.0."
    )
    angular_z: float = Field(
        ...,
        ge=-2.0,
        le=2.0,
        description="Rotational velocity setpoint (rad/s). Clamped between -2.0 and +2.0."
    )

    @field_validator('linear_x', 'angular_z')
    @classmethod
    def check_finite(cls, v: float) -> float:
        if math.isnan(v) or math.isinf(v):
            raise ValueError("Velocity cannot be NaN or Infinite.")
        return v


class NavigationGoalPayload(BaseModel):
    """Payload for dispatching an autonomous navigation waypoint."""
    x: float = Field(..., ge=-50.0, le=50.0, description="Target X coordinate in map frame (m).")
    y: float = Field(..., ge=-50.0, le=50.0, description="Target Y coordinate in map frame (m).")
    yaw: float = Field(0.0, ge=-math.pi, le=math.pi, description="Target orientation yaw angle (rad).")


class SystemHealthResponse(BaseModel):
    """System health snapshot response."""
    robot_id: str = "navpro-mini-amr"
    status: str
    is_online: bool
    battery_percentage: float
    estop_active: bool
    current_position: Dict[str, float]
    ros2_connected: bool
    timestamp: float

4. Mounting the REST Endpoints

PYTHON
from fastapi import APIRouter, HTTPException, status
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist

router = APIRouter(prefix="/api/v1", tags=["Robotics Core APIs"])


@router.get("/system/health", response_model=SystemHealthResponse)
async def get_system_health():
    """Returns real-time health, connectivity, and battery status."""
    snapshot = robot_state.get_snapshot()
    return SystemHealthResponse(
        robot_id="navpro-mini-amr",
        status="ESTOP" if snapshot["emergency_stop"] else "OPERATIONAL",
        is_online=True,
        battery_percentage=snapshot["battery_percentage"],
        estop_active=snapshot["emergency_stop"],
        current_position={
            "x": round(snapshot["x"], 3),
            "y": round(snapshot["y"], 3),
            "yaw": round(snapshot["yaw"], 3)
        },
        ros2_connected=rclpy.ok(),
        timestamp=snapshot["timestamp"]
    )


@router.post("/teleop", status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK)
async def manual_teleop(cmd: TeleopPayload):
    """Publishes velocity commands to the ROS 2 /cmd_vel topic."""
    snapshot = robot_state.get_snapshot()
    if snapshot["emergency_stop"]:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_409_CONFLICT,
            detail="Cannot execute teleop: Hardware Emergency Stop is currently ENGAGED!"
        )

    # Publish Twist to ROS 2
    twist = Twist()
    twist.linear.x = float(cmd.linear_x)
    twist.angular.z = float(cmd.angular_z)
    ros2_node.cmd_vel_pub.publish(twist)

    return {"status": "COMMAND_ACCEPTED", "linear_x": cmd.linear_x, "angular_z": cmd.angular_z}


@router.post("/emergency_stop", status_code=status.HTTP_200_OK)
async def trigger_emergency_stop():
    """Immediately stops the robot and engages software E-Stop."""
    zero_twist = Twist()
    for _ in range(5):
        ros2_node.cmd_vel_pub.publish(zero_twist)

    robot_state.set_estop(True)
    return {"status": "ESTOP_ENGAGED", "detail": "Motors cut off immediately."}

In this lesson, you built the core REST API Gateway:

  • Configured FastAPI with @asynccontextmanager lifespan for background ROS 2 management.
  • Enforced physical velocity limits using Pydantic v2 schemas.
  • Protected the robot from invalid inputs with automated 422 error responses.

Lesson 06: High-Frequency 20Hz WebSocket Telemetry Broadcaster

In Lesson 05, we built the REST endpoints. Now, we implement the real-time engine: the 20Hz WebSocket Broadcaster.

In an autonomous warehouse, multiple client devices (the supervisor's desktop cockpit, floor tablets, and wearable smartwatch badges) must track the robot's physical movement simultaneously.

In this lesson, you will build a scalable ConnectionManager and an asyncio 20Hz broadcast worker that streams odometry snapshots to all connected clients.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Implement an asynchronous ConnectionManager handling multiple concurrent client sockets.
  2. Schedule a high-precision 20Hz ($50\,\text{ms}$) broadcast loop using Python asyncio.
  3. Ingest mutex-protected cache snapshots and serialize clean telemetry JSON frames.
  4. Detect disconnected clients and prune dead sockets to prevent memory leaks.
  5. Verify live streaming using terminal tools (websocat) and browser JavaScript.

2. Multi-Client WebSocket Architecture

MERMAID
graph TD
    Cache[("ThreadSafeRobotState Cache (Updated at 50Hz by /odom)")]
    Worker["20Hz Broadcast Worker (asyncio.sleep 0.05s)"]
    Manager["ConnectionManager (Active Socket Pool)"]
    
    C1["Client 1: Desktop Fleet Cockpit"]
    C2["Client 2: Floor Operator Tablet"]
    C3["Client 3: Smartwatch Wearable Badge"]

    Cache -->|Atomic Read| Worker
    Worker -->|JSON Frame| Manager
    Manager -->|Push Frame| C1
    Manager -->|Push Frame| C2
    Manager -->|Push Frame| C3

3. Implementing the ConnectionManager

PYTHON
import asyncio
import json
import logging
from typing import Set, Dict, Any
from fastapi import WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect

logger = logging.getLogger("WebSocketBroadcaster")


class ConnectionManager:
    """Maintains active WebSocket clients and broadcasts telemetry frames."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.active_connections: Set[WebSocket] = set()
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def connect(self, websocket: WebSocket):
        """Accepts and registers incoming client socket."""
        await websocket.accept()
        async with self._lock:
            self.active_connections.add(websocket)
        logger.info(f"WebSocket client connected. Total clients: {len(self.active_connections)}")

    async def disconnect(self, websocket: WebSocket):
        """Removes disconnected socket."""
        async with self._lock:
            self.active_connections.discard(websocket)
        logger.info(f"WebSocket client removed. Remaining clients: {len(self.active_connections)}")

    async def broadcast_json(self, frame: Dict[str, Any]):
        """Pushes JSON payload to all active clients concurrently."""
        if not self.active_connections:
            return

        payload_str = json.dumps(frame)
        stale_clients = []

        async with self._lock:
            clients_snapshot = list(self.active_connections)

        for ws in clients_snapshot:
            try:
                await ws.send_text(payload_str)
            except Exception:
                stale_clients.append(ws)

        if stale_clients:
            async with self._lock:
                for ws in stale_clients:
                    self.active_connections.discard(ws)
            logger.warning(f"Pruned {len(stale_clients)} dead WebSocket sockets.")

4. Building the 20Hz Broadcast Loop

Inside FastAPI's lifespan, we spawn the background broadcaster:

PYTHON
ws_manager = ConnectionManager()


async def telemetry_broadcast_worker():
    """Extracts state every 50ms (20Hz) and broadcasts to all web clients."""
    logger.info("20Hz Telemetry Broadcast Worker started.")
    while True:
        try:
            # 1. Fetch latest snapshot from thread-safe cache
            snapshot = robot_state.get_snapshot()

            # 2. Construct clean JSON frame
            telemetry_frame = {
                "type": "TELEMETRY_FRAME",
                "robot_id": "navpro-mini-amr",
                "x": round(snapshot["x"], 3),
                "y": round(snapshot["y"], 3),
                "yaw": round(snapshot["yaw"], 3),
                "linear_v": round(snapshot["linear_velocity"], 2),
                "angular_w": round(snapshot["angular_velocity"], 2),
                "battery": round(snapshot["battery_percentage"], 1),
                "estop": snapshot["emergency_stop"],
                "timestamp": round(snapshot["timestamp"], 3)
            }

            # 3. Broadcast to all connected dashboards
            await ws_manager.broadcast_json(telemetry_frame)

        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Error in telemetry broadcast worker: {e}")

        # Sleep exactly 50ms (20Hz)
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)


@app.websocket("/ws/telemetry")
async def websocket_telemetry_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket):
    """WebSocket route accessed by Cockpit UI and Smartwatch."""
    await ws_manager.connect(websocket)
    try:
        while True:
            # Keep socket open and listen for ping heartbeats
            client_msg = await websocket.receive_text()
            if client_msg == "PING":
                await websocket.send_text('{"type": "PONG"}')
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        await ws_manager.disconnect(websocket)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning(f"Socket dropped: {e}")
        await ws_manager.disconnect(websocket)

lessons.html_content:
Lesson 07: Non-Blocking Nav2 Action Dispatching — HTTP 202 Accepted

In Lesson 06, we built the real-time streaming pipe. Now, we tackle long-running physical tasks: Autonomous Waypoint Navigation.

When an AMR drives across a warehouse, the navigation maneuver may take $15$ to $90$ seconds. If an HTTP endpoint (POST /api/v1/navigation/goal) blocks waiting for the robot to arrive:

  1. The web client's request will time out with an HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout.
  2. The web connection remains locked, exhausting server socket pools.
  3. The client cannot send cancellation requests or monitor live progress.

In this lesson, you will learn the Asynchronous Action Dispatch Pattern, mapping ROS 2 Actions into non-blocking HTTP 202 Accepted workflows.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Explain why synchronous HTTP request-response fails for physical robotics navigation.
  2. Implement the HTTP 202 Accepted pattern with tracking goal_id tokens.
  3. Wrap rclpy.action.ActionClient for nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose inside async Python routines.
  4. Build a state tracker for active navigation goals (ACCEPTED, EXECUTING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, CANCELED).
  5. Implement safe cancellation endpoints (POST /api/v1/navigation/cancel/{goal_id}).

2. The Asynchronous Action Dispatch Pattern

Instead of blocking the HTTP connection, we decouple goal initiation from goal monitoring:

MERMAID
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Web as Web Client / Cockpit
    participant API as FastAPI Gateway
    participant Bridge as Action Dispatcher
    participant Nav2 as ROS 2 Nav2 Action Server

    Web->>API: POST /api/v1/navigation/goal {x: 12.5, y: -4.0}
    API->>Bridge: Validate & Dispatch (Generate UUID: 'nav_98a')
    Bridge->>Nav2: send_goal_async(NavigateToPose)
    API-->>Web: HTTP 202 Accepted {goal_id: 'nav_98a', status: 'ACCEPTED'}
    Note over Web,API: HTTP transaction finishes in < 15ms!

    loop Periodic Status Polling (or via WebSocket)
        Web->>API: GET /api/v1/navigation/status/nav_98a
        API-->>Web: HTTP 200 OK {status: 'EXECUTING', distance_remaining: 3.2m}
    end

    Nav2-->>Bridge: Goal Result: SUCCEEDED
    Bridge->>API: Update goal status cache: 'SUCCEEDED'
    Web->>API: GET /api/v1/navigation/status/nav_98a
    API-->>Web: HTTP 200 OK {status: 'SUCCEEDED', error_code: 0}

3. Implementing the Goal Registry

We maintain an in-memory registry tracking the lifecycle of all submitted navigation jobs:

PYTHON
import uuid
import time
from enum import Enum
from typing import Dict, Any, Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel


class GoalState(str, Enum):
    ACCEPTED = "ACCEPTED"
    EXECUTING = "EXECUTING"
    SUCCEEDED = "SUCCEEDED"
    FAILED = "FAILED"
    CANCELED = "CANCELED"


class NavigationJob(BaseModel):
    goal_id: str
    target_x: float
    target_y: float
    target_yaw: float
    status: GoalState
    created_at: float
    completed_at: Optional[float] = None
    error_message: Optional[str] = None


class GoalRegistry:
    """Thread-safe registry tracking active and completed navigation tasks."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._jobs: Dict[str, NavigationJob] = {}

    def create_job(self, x: float, y: float, yaw: float) -> str:
        goal_id = f"nav_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}"
        job = NavigationJob(
            goal_id=goal_id,
            target_x=x,
            target_y=y,
            target_yaw=yaw,
            status=GoalState.ACCEPTED,
            created_at=time.time()
        )
        self._jobs[goal_id] = job
        return goal_id

    def update_status(self, goal_id: str, status: GoalState, error: Optional[str] = None):
        if goal_id in self._jobs:
            self._jobs[goal_id].status = status
            if status in (GoalState.SUCCEEDED, GoalState.FAILED, GoalState.CANCELED):
                self._jobs[goal_id].completed_at = time.time()
            if error:
                self._jobs[goal_id].error_message = error

    def get_job(self, goal_id: str) -> Optional[NavigationJob]:
        return self._jobs.get(goal_id)

4. Wrapping the Nav2 Action Client

PYTHON
from rclpy.action import ActionClient
from nav2_msgs.action import NavigateToPose
from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped
import math

class Nav2BridgeNode(Node):
    def __init__(self, registry: GoalRegistry):
        super().__init__('nav2_bridge_node')
        self.registry = registry
        self.action_client = ActionClient(self, NavigateToPose, 'navigate_to_pose')
        self.active_goal_handle = None

    def dispatch_navigation_goal(self, goal_id: str, x: float, y: float, yaw: float):
        """Asynchronously dispatches goal to Nav2 without blocking."""
        if not self.action_client.wait_for_server(timeout_sec=2.0):
            self.registry.update_status(goal_id, GoalState.FAILED, "Nav2 Action Server not available")
            return

        goal_msg = NavigateToPose.Goal()
        goal_msg.pose.header.frame_id = 'map'
        goal_msg.pose.header.stamp = self.get_clock().now().to_msg()
        goal_msg.pose.pose.position.x = float(x)
        goal_msg.pose.pose.position.y = float(y)
        
        # Quaternion calculation
        goal_msg.pose.pose.orientation.z = math.sin(yaw / 2.0)
        goal_msg.pose.pose.orientation.w = math.cos(yaw / 2.0)

        # Send goal asynchronously
        send_future = self.action_client.send_goal_async(goal_msg)
        send_future.add_done_callback(lambda future: self._goal_response_callback(future, goal_id))

    def _goal_response_callback(self, future, goal_id: str):
        goal_handle = future.result()
        if not goal_handle.accepted:
            self.registry.update_status(goal_id, GoalState.FAILED, "Nav2 rejected navigation goal")
            return

        self.active_goal_handle = goal_handle
        self.registry.update_status(goal_id, GoalState.EXECUTING)
        
        result_future = goal_handle.get_result_async()
        result_future.add_done_callback(lambda res_fut: self._goal_result_callback(res_fut, goal_id))

    def _goal_result_callback(self, future, goal_id: str):
        result = future.result()
        # ROS 2 GoalStatus: 4 = SUCCEEDED, 5 = CANCELED
        if result.status == 4:
            self.registry.update_status(goal_id, GoalState.SUCCEEDED)
        elif result.status == 5:
            self.registry.update_status(goal_id, GoalState.CANCELED)
        else:
            self.registry.update_status(goal_id, GoalState.FAILED, f"Nav2 returned status code: {result.status}")
        self.active_goal_handle = None

    def cancel_active_goal(self, goal_id: str) -> bool:
        if self.active_goal_handle:
            self.active_goal_handle.cancel_goal_async()
            self.registry.update_status(goal_id, GoalState.CANCELED)
            return True
        return False

5. Exposing Endpoints in FastAPI

PYTHON
@app.post("/api/v1/navigation/goal", status_code=status.HTTP_202_ACCEPTED)
async def dispatch_goal(payload: NavigationGoalPayload):
    """Submits a navigation goal and returns HTTP 202 Accepted immediately."""
    goal_id = goal_registry.create_job(payload.x, payload.y, payload.yaw)
    nav2_node.dispatch_navigation_goal(goal_id, payload.x, payload.y, payload.yaw)

    return {
        "status": "ACCEPTED",
        "goal_id": goal_id,
        "message": "Navigation goal accepted and dispatched to Nav2.",
        "status_url": f"/api/v1/navigation/status/{goal_id}"
    }


@app.get("/api/v1/navigation/status/{goal_id}")
async def get_goal_status(goal_id: str):
    """Retrieves current execution status of a navigation job."""
    job = goal_registry.get_job(goal_id)
    if not job:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Navigation goal ID not found.")
    return job


@app.post("/api/v1/navigation/cancel/{goal_id}")
async def cancel_goal(goal_id: str):
    """Cancels an in-progress navigation goal."""
    success = nav2_node.cancel_active_goal(goal_id)
    if not success:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Unable to cancel goal (not active or completed).")
    return {"status": "CANCEL_REQUESTED", "goal_id": goal_id}

6. Summary & Next Steps

In this lesson, you mastered non-blocking action handling:

  • Replaced fragile synchronous HTTP requests with the HTTP 202 Accepted pattern.
  • Tracked full navigation lifecycles using unique goal_id identifiers.
  • Implemented cancellation hooks to safely abort autonomous motion in real time.

In Lesson 08, you will combine everything built in Day 1 into our Day 1 Capstone Project: The Production NavPro API Gateway!

lessons.title: Client SDK Architecture — Building Python & JavaScript Robotics SDKs
lessons.html_content:
Lesson 09: Client SDK Architecture — Building Python & JavaScript Robotics SDKs

Welcome to Day 2 of the Level 2 Advanced Robotics Workshop! On Day 1, you built a high-performance REST and WebSocket API Gateway.

However, in professional software engineering, frontend web applications, mobile apps, and automated scripts never make raw fetch() or curl calls directly to individual endpoints. If an endpoint URL changes or an authentication header format is updated, every screen across the codebase breaks.

Instead, companies build a Client SDK (Software Development Kit). In this lesson, you will learn the architecture of robotics client SDKs (modeled after the production navpromini_sdk and Dart SdkApiService), building clean, reusable Python and JavaScript client libraries.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the architectural advantages of an SDK over ad-hoc raw HTTP/WebSocket requests.
  2. Design a standardized, object-oriented client interface: get_health(), teleop(), navigate(), and on_telemetry().
  3. Handle network timeouts, graceful reconnects, and structured exceptions (RobotApiException).
  4. Implement a production Python SDK using httpx and websockets.
  5. Implement a lightweight JavaScript client SDK for browser frontends.

2. Client SDK Architecture

The SDK encapsulates the complexity of HTTP requests, authentication tokens, JSON serialization, and persistent WebSocket streams behind a clean, developer-friendly class:

MERMAID
graph LR
    subgraph Client_Applications["Client Code (Clean & Readable)"]
        UI["Fleet Cockpit Web App"]
        Script["Python Automation Script"]
    end

    subgraph NavPro_SDK["NavPro Client SDK (Abstraction Layer)"]
        Client["NavProClient(host='192.168.1.100')"]
        HTTPHandler["_send(method, path, body)"]
        WSHandler["_stream_telemetry(callback)"]
        AuthHandler["Bearer Token Injection"]
    end

    subgraph Robot_Backend["Robot Gateway (Port 8080)"]
        REST["FastAPI REST Endpoints"]
        WS["20Hz Telemetry WebSocket"]
    end

    UI -->|client.teleop(0.5, 0.0)| Client
    Script -->|client.navigate(4.2, 1.5)| Client

    Client --> HTTPHandler
    Client --> WSHandler
    HTTPHandler --> AuthHandler

    AuthHandler -->|HTTP / JSON| REST
    WSHandler -->|WebSocket Frames| WS

3. Designing the Python Client SDK (navpro_client.py)

Here is the production implementation of the Python SDK:

PYTHON
import time
import json
import asyncio
import threading
from typing import Dict, Any, Callable, Optional
import httpx
import websockets


class RobotApiException(Exception):
    """Raised when the robot gateway returns a non-2xx status code or network fails."""
    def __init__(self, status_code: int, message: str, detail: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None):
        self.status_code = status_code
        self.message = message
        self.detail = detail or {}
        super().__init__(f"[{status_code}] {message}: {self.detail}")


class NavProClient:
    """Client SDK for interfacing with NavPro robots over REST and WebSockets."""

    def __init__(self, host: str = "localhost", port: int = 8080, api_token: Optional[str] = None):
        self.base_url = f"http://{host}:{port}"
        self.ws_url = f"ws://{host}:{port}/ws/telemetry"
        self.headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json"}
        if api_token:
            self.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {api_token}"
        self._http = httpx.Client(base_url=self.base_url, timeout=5.0)

    # 1. Health & Status
    def get_health(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Fetches robot health, connectivity, and battery state."""
        resp = self._http.get("/api/v1/system/health", headers=self.headers)
        if resp.status_code != 200:
            raise RobotApiException(resp.status_code, "Failed to fetch health", resp.json())
        return resp.json()

    # 2. Velocity Teleoperation
    def send_velocity(self, linear_x: float, angular_z: float) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Sends velocity setpoint to robot /cmd_vel."""
        payload = {"linear_x": float(linear_x), "angular_z": float(angular_z)}
        resp = self._http.post("/api/v1/teleop", json=payload, headers=self.headers)
        if resp.status_code != 200:
            raise RobotApiException(resp.status_code, "Teleop command rejected", resp.json())
        return resp.json()

    # 3. Autonomous Waypoint Navigation
    def navigate_to_coordinates(self, x: float, y: float, yaw: float = 0.0) -> str:
        """Dispatches autonomous navigation goal and returns tracking goal_id."""
        payload = {"x": float(x), "y": float(y), "yaw": float(yaw)}
        resp = self._http.post("/api/v1/navigation/goal", json=payload, headers=self.headers)
        if resp.status_code != 202:
            raise RobotApiException(resp.status_code, "Navigation goal rejected", resp.json())
        return resp.json()["goal_id"]

    # 4. Emergency Stop
    def emergency_stop(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Triggers immediate hardware emergency stop."""
        resp = self._http.post("/api/v1/emergency_stop", headers=self.headers)
        return resp.json()

    # 5. Live Telemetry Streaming (WebSocket Thread)
    def start_telemetry_listener(self, on_frame_callback: Callable[[Dict[str, Any]], None]):
        """Spawns background thread streaming 20Hz telemetry over WebSockets."""
        async def ws_loop():
            while True:
                try:
                    async with websockets.connect(self.ws_url) as ws:
                        while True:
                            msg = await ws.recv()
                            data = json.loads(msg)
                            on_frame_callback(data)
                except Exception as e:
                    await asyncio.sleep(2.0) # Retry on disconnect

        def run_loop():
            asyncio.run(ws_loop())

        t = threading.Thread(target=run_loop, daemon=True, name="NavPro-WS-Listener")
        t.start()
        return t

4. Designing the JavaScript SDK (navpro_client.js)

For web browsers and the Cockpit GUI, we implement the equivalent JavaScript class:

JAVASCRIPT
class NavProWebClient {
    constructor(host = "localhost", port = 8080) {
        this.baseUrl = `http://${host}:${port}`;
        this.wsUrl = `ws://${host}:${port}/ws/telemetry`;
        this.ws = null;
    }

    async getHealth() {
        const res = await fetch(`${this.baseUrl}/api/v1/system/health`);
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Health check failed: ${res.statusText}`);
        return await res.json();
    }

    async sendVelocity(linearX, angularZ) {
        const res = await fetch(`${this.baseUrl}/api/v1/teleop`, {
            method: "POST",
            headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
            body: JSON.stringify({ linear_x: linearX, angular_z: angularZ })
        });
        return await res.json();
    }

    async navigate(x, y, yaw = 0.0) {
        const res = await fetch(`${this.baseUrl}/api/v1/navigation/goal`, {
            method: "POST",
            headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
            body: JSON.stringify({ x, y, yaw })
        });
        const data = await res.json();
        return data.goal_id;
    }

    async emergencyStop() {
        const res = await fetch(`${this.baseUrl}/api/v1/emergency_stop`, { method: "POST" });
        return await res.json();
    }

    connectTelemetry(onFrameCallback) {
        this.ws = new WebSocket(this.wsUrl);
        this.ws.onmessage = (event) => {
            const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
            if (data.type === "TELEMETRY_FRAME") {
                onFrameCallback(data);
            }
        };
        this.ws.onclose = () => {
            setTimeout(() => this.connectTelemetry(onFrameCallback), 2000); // Auto reconnect
        };
    }
}

5. Summary & Next Steps

In this lesson, you designed clean Client SDKs:

  • Abstracted network protocol details behind simple class methods.
  • Built reusable Python and JavaScript client SDKs.
  • Handled network errors and automatic WebSocket reconnection.

In Lesson 10, we will use this SDK to build the Modern Fleet Cockpit UI, mastering multi-layer Canvas rendering and coordinate transforms!

lessons.html_content:
Lesson 10: Modern Fleet Cockpit UI Architecture — Multi-Layer Canvas & Coordinates

In Lesson 09, we built our Client SDKs. Now, we begin constructing the frontend operator surface: The Modern Fleet Cockpit GUI.

When building robotics dashboards, the most common engineering mistake is treating a robotics map like a standard web page. If you attempt to render a $2000 \times 2000$ SLAM occupancy grid inside an HTML <img> tag or redraw the entire DOM at $20\,\text{Hz}$, the browser tab will freeze and drop frames.

In this lesson, you will learn the Multi-Layer Canvas Architecture and master the mathematical transformation between ROS Metric Frames and HTML5 Screen Pixels.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the performance advantages of Multi-Layer Canvas Architecture over single-layer DOM rendering.
  2. Differentiate between the ROS 2 Metric Coordinate Frame (Right-handed, $+X$ Forward, $+Y$ Left) and the HTML5 Canvas Frame ($+X$ Right, $+Y$ Down).
  3. Derive and implement the mathematical transformation formula mapping world meters to screen pixels.
  4. Implement pan and zoom viewport navigation (scaling and translation offsets).
  5. Structure a modern HTML5/CSS3 robotics cockpit layout.

2. Multi-Layer Canvas Architecture

In high-performance cockpits (like RViz, Foxglove Studio, and the NavPro Cockpit), the viewport is split into three independent visual layers:

MERMAID
graph TD
    subgraph Viewport["Cockpit Multi-Layer Canvas Viewport"]
        L3["Layer 3 (Top DOM): Interactive UI Controls (Joystick, Buttons, Gates)"]
        L2["Layer 2 (Middle Canvas): Dynamic Entities (Robot Pose, Lidar, Nav2 Path at 60 FPS)"]
        L1["Layer 1 (Bottom Canvas): Static SLAM Map (Occupancy Grid Bitmap)"]
    end

    subgraph Data["Update Frequencies"]
        D1["Map: Redrawn ONLY on pan/zoom or new map load"]
        D2["Pose/Path: Redrawn at 60 FPS using requestAnimationFrame"]
        D3["UI: Standard DOM event listeners (click, touch)"]
    end

    D1 --> L1
    D2 --> L2
    D3 --> L3
  • Bottom Canvas (Layer 1): Renders the static SLAM grid. Decoded once into an off-screen bitmap.
  • Middle Canvas (Layer 2): Cleared and redrawn at 60 FPS. Renders the robot marker, heading vector, footprint, and Nav2 planned path.
  • Top DOM (Layer 3): Standard HTML/CSS buttons, virtual joysticks, and modal dialogs.

3. The Coordinate Transformation Problem

ROS 2 coordinate frames (defined by REP-105) follow standard mathematical conventions:

  • $+X$ points forward (East).
  • $+Y$ points left (North).
  • Yaw angle $\theta$ rotates counter-clockwise.
  • Units are strictly in meters.

HTML5 Canvas uses a computer graphics coordinate frame:

  • Origin $(0, 0)$ is at the top-left corner.
  • $+X$ points right.
  • $+Y$ points downward.
  • Yaw angle $\theta$ rotates clockwise.
  • Units are strictly in pixels.
BASH
    ROS 2 World Frame (Meters):          Canvas Screen Frame (Pixels):
            +Y (Left / North)                     (0, 0) ───────> +X (Right)
                 ▲                                  │
                 │                                  │
                 └──────> +X (Forward)              ▼ +Y (Down)

4. The World-to-Screen Mathematical Formula

To convert any point $(x_{\text{world}}, y_{\text{world}})$ into screen pixels $(x_{\text{screen}}, y_{\text{screen}})$:

$$x_{\text{screen}} = \text{pan}_x + (x_{\text{world}} - \text{origin}_x) \cdot \text{scale}$$

$$y_{\text{screen}} = \text{pan}_y - (y_{\text{world}} - \text{origin}_y) \cdot \text{scale}$$

Where:

  • $\text{scale}$ is the zoom factor in pixels per meter (e.g. $25\,\text{px/m}$).
  • $\text{origin}_x, \text{origin}_y$ is the map origin offset in meters.
  • $\text{pan}_x, \text{pan}_y$ is the canvas pan offset in pixels (usually canvas center: $\text{width}/2, \text{height}/2$).
  • Notice the minus sign ($-$) in $y_{\text{screen}}$: this inverts the vertical axis so $+Y$ points up!

5. Implementing the Coordinate Transformer in JavaScript

JAVASCRIPT
class CoordinateTransformer {
    constructor(canvasWidth, canvasHeight) {
        this.scale = 25.0; // 25 pixels per meter
        this.panX = canvasWidth / 2;
        this.panY = canvasHeight / 2;
        this.mapOriginX = 0.0;
        this.mapOriginY = 0.0;
    }

    worldToScreen(worldX, worldY) {
        const screenX = this.panX + (worldX - this.mapOriginX) * this.scale;
        const screenY = this.panY - (worldY - this.mapOriginY) * this.scale;
        return { x: screenX, y: screenY };
    }

    screenToWorld(screenX, screenY) {
        const worldX = ((screenX - this.panX) / this.scale) + this.mapOriginX;
        const worldY = -((screenY - this.panY) / this.scale) + this.mapOriginY;
        return { x: worldX, y: worldY };
    }

    zoom(delta, cursorX, cursorY) {
        const factor = delta > 0 ? 1.15 : 0.85;
        this.scale = Math.max(5.0, Math.min(200.0, this.scale * factor));
    }

    pan(dx, dy) {
        this.panX += dx;
        this.panY += dy;
    }
}

6. Summary & Next Steps

In this lesson, you designed the Cockpit architecture:

  • Adopted the Multi-Layer Canvas Architecture to preserve 60 FPS performance.
  • Mastered the mathematical conversion between ROS metric space and Canvas screen pixels.
  • Built the CoordinateTransformer class supporting pan and zoom.

In Lesson 11, we will decode and render the 2D SLAM Occupancy Grid Map on Canvas Layer 1!

Lesson 11: Rendering the 2D SLAM Map — Occupancy Grids on HTML5 Canvas

In Lesson 10, we implemented coordinate transforms. Now, we will render the physical foundation of autonomous navigation: The 2D SLAM Occupancy Grid Map.

In ROS 2, mapping packages like slam_toolbox and cartographer publish maps as nav_msgs/msg/OccupancyGrid. To visualize this map in a browser cockpit, we must decode this 1D array of probability numbers into RGBA pixels and render them on an off-screen canvas.

In this lesson, you will master the structure of ROS 2 Occupancy Grids and build an efficient JavaScript renderer.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Deconstruct the ROS 2 nav_msgs/msg/OccupancyGrid message: resolution, width, height, origin, and data.
  2. Map occupancy values ($-1$, $0$, $100$) into visual color palettes (Unknown, Free space, Lethal obstacles).
  3. Convert a 1D row-major array into an HTML5 ImageData RGBA buffer (Uint8ClampedArray).
  4. Cache decoded maps onto an off-screen canvas to eliminate redrawing lag.
  5. Render the scaled, aligned map onto the cockpit screen.

2. Anatomy of an Occupancy Grid

In ROS 2, an OccupancyGrid represents 2D space as a discrete grid of square cells:

MERMAID
graph TD
    Map["nav_msgs/msg/OccupancyGrid"]
    Info["info: MapMetaData"]
    Data["data: int8[] (1D Array of size width * height)"]

    Info --> Res["resolution: 0.05m (5cm per cell)"]
    Info --> Dim["width: 400 cells, height: 400 cells"]
    Info --> Orig["origin: Pose (x: -10.0m, y: -10.0m)"]

    Data --> ValUnknown["-1: Unknown / Unexplored Space"]
    Data --> ValFree["0: Free / Traversable Space"]
    Data --> ValObstacle["100: Lethal Wall / Obstacle"]

Color Palette Mapping

Value in Grid Cell State Hex Color Visual Appearance
-1 Unknown Space #94a3b8 Medium gray background.
0 Free Space #ffffff Pure white (robot can drive here).
1 to 99 Dynamic Gradient #e2e8f0 → #334155 Gradual grayscale based on occupancy probability.
100 Lethal Obstacle #0f172a Deep black/slate (walls, furniture, columns).

3. Decoding 1D Row-Major Data into RGBA Pixels

The data array is serialized in row-major order: row 0 (bottom-left) to row $H-1$ (top-right).

HTML5 Canvas expects an ImageData array where every cell occupies 4 contiguous bytes: [Red, Green, Blue, Alpha]:

JAVASCRIPT
function decodeOccupancyGridToImageData(grid) {
    const width = grid.width;
    const height = grid.height;
    const data = grid.data; // 1D array of numbers [-1, 100]

    // Create an off-screen RGBA image buffer (4 bytes per cell)
    const imgData = new ImageData(width, height);
    const pixels = imgData.data;

    for (let row = 0; row < height; row++) {
        for (let col = 0; col < width; col++) {
            // ROS 2 row 0 is at bottom; Canvas row 0 is at top -> Invert Y row index
            const rosIndex = row * width + col;
            const canvasIndex = ((height - 1 - row) * width + col) * 4;

            const val = data[rosIndex];

            if (val === -1) {
                // Unknown space: Slate Gray (#94a3b8)
                pixels[canvasIndex] = 148;     // R
                pixels[canvasIndex + 1] = 163; // G
                pixels[canvasIndex + 2] = 184; // B
                pixels[canvasIndex + 3] = 255; // Alpha
            } else if (val === 0) {
                // Free space: White (#ffffff)
                pixels[canvasIndex] = 255;
                pixels[canvasIndex + 1] = 255;
                pixels[canvasIndex + 2] = 255;
                pixels[canvasIndex + 3] = 255;
            } else {
                // Obstacle (val > 0): Dark Slate (#0f172a)
                pixels[canvasIndex] = 15;
                pixels[canvasIndex + 1] = 23;
                pixels[canvasIndex + 2] = 42;
                pixels[canvasIndex + 3] = 255;
            }
        }
    }

    return imgData;
}

4. Off-Screen Canvas Caching Pattern

Once decoded, we draw the ImageData onto a dedicated off-screen canvas. When the operator pans or zooms, the browser simply blits the pre-rendered image buffer at hardware-accelerated speeds:

JAVASCRIPT
class MapLayerRenderer {
    constructor() {
        this.offscreenCanvas = document.createElement("canvas");
        this.offscreenCtx = this.offscreenCanvas.getContext("2d");
        this.isLoaded = false;
        this.gridInfo = null;
    }

    loadGrid(gridData) {
        this.gridInfo = gridData.info;
        this.offscreenCanvas.width = this.gridInfo.width;
        this.offscreenCanvas.height = this.gridInfo.height;

        const imgData = decodeOccupancyGridToImageData(gridData);
        this.offscreenCtx.putImageData(imgData, 0, 0);
        this.isLoaded = true;
    }

    render(ctx, transformer) {
        if (!this.isLoaded) return;

        // Calculate screen bounding box for the map image
        const resolution = this.gridInfo.resolution; // e.g. 0.05 m/cell
        const originX = this.gridInfo.origin.x;
        const originY = this.gridInfo.origin.y;

        // Lower-left corner in screen coordinates
        const pt = transformer.worldToScreen(originX, originY);
        
        const renderWidth = this.gridInfo.width * resolution * transformer.scale;
        const renderHeight = this.gridInfo.height * resolution * transformer.scale;

        // Draw cached bitmap
        ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = false; // Keep sharp crisp pixelated walls
        ctx.drawImage(this.offscreenCanvas, pt.x, pt.y - renderHeight, renderWidth, renderHeight);
    }
}

5. Summary & Next Steps

In this lesson, you mastered 2D SLAM map rendering:

  • Decoded the ROS 2 OccupancyGrid structure.
  • Mapped $-1, 0, 100$ into clean, modern color palettes.
  • Used off-screen canvas caching to render gigabyte grids with zero stutter.

In Lesson 12, we will build Layer 2: Rendering the Live Robot Pose, Heading & Planned Nav2 Paths at 60 FPS!

Lesson 12: Live Robot Pose & Trajectory Rendering at 60 FPS

In Lesson 11, we decoded and rendered the static SLAM Occupancy Grid on Canvas Layer 1.

Now, we build the dynamic entity layer: Canvas Layer 2. This layer runs a smooth $60\,\text{FPS}$ render loop (requestAnimationFrame), updating the robot's physical position, heading vector, circular chassis footprint, and the planned Nav2 global trajectory.

1. Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. Implement a 60 FPS rendering loop using requestAnimationFrame.
  2. Clear and redraw dynamic entities without affecting the cached map underneath.
  3. Draw metric robot features: AMR circular footprint, orientation pointer, and safety inflation buffer.
  4. Render Nav2 global path trajectories (nav_msgs/msg/Path) as styled spline paths.
  5. Maintain a dynamic breadcrumb trail visualizing the robot's historical path.

2. Dynamic Entity Rendering Architecture

While telemetry arrives over WebSockets at $20\,\text{Hz}$ ($50\,\text{ms}$ intervals), web displays refresh at $60\,\text{Hz}$ ($16.6\,\text{ms}$). By interpolating between telemetry frames inside requestAnimationFrame, the robot marker glides smoothly across the map with zero micro-stuttering:

MERMAID
graph TD
    WS["20Hz Telemetry WebSocket"]
    State["Latest Pose: (x, y, yaw)"]
    RAF["Browser requestAnimationFrame Loop (60 FPS)"]
    Layer2["Layer 2 Canvas Context"]

    WS -->|Update snapshot every 50ms| State
    RAF -->|Clear Rect & Draw 60 times/sec| Layer2
    State --> RAF

    subgraph Draw_Steps["Layer 2 Draw Sequence"]
        S1["1. Draw Historical Breadcrumb Trail"]
        S2["2. Draw Nav2 Planned Global Path"]
        S3["3. Draw AMR Chassis & Footprint"]
        S4["4. Draw Heading Vector & Safety Ring"]
    end

    Layer2 --> Draw_Steps

3. Implementing the 60 FPS Robot Renderer in JavaScript

JAVASCRIPT
class DynamicEntityRenderer {
    constructor(canvasId, transformer) {
        this.canvas = document.getElementById(canvasId);
        this.ctx = this.canvas.getContext("2d");
        this.transformer = transformer;

        // Active State
        this.currentPose = { x: 0.0, y: 0.0, yaw: 0.0 };
        this.plannedPath = [];
        this.trailHistory = [];
        this.maxTrailLength = 200;

        // Robot physical dimensions in meters
        this.robotRadius = 0.22; // 22cm radius (NavPro Mini chassis)
    }

    updateTelemetry(telemetry) {
        this.currentPose.x = telemetry.x;
        this.currentPose.y = telemetry.y;
        this.currentPose.yaw = telemetry.yaw;

        // Append to breadcrumb trail
        this.trailHistory.push({ x: telemetry.x, y: telemetry.y });
        if (this.trailHistory.length > this.maxTrailLength) {
            this.trailHistory.shift();
        }
    }

    updatePlannedPath(pathWaypoints) {
        this.plannedPath = pathWaypoints; // Array of {x, y}
    }

    render() {
        // Clear only the dynamic layer (Map layer beneath remains intact!)
        this.ctx.clearRect(0, 0, this.canvas.width, this.canvas.height);

        // 1. Draw Breadcrumb History Trail
        if (this.trailHistory.length > 1) {
            this.ctx.strokeStyle = "rgba(2, 132, 199, 0.3)";
            this.ctx.lineWidth = 2;
            this.ctx.beginPath();
            for (let i = 0; i < this.trailHistory.length; i++) {
                const pt = this.transformer.worldToScreen(this.trailHistory[i].x, this.trailHistory[i].y);
                if (i === 0) this.ctx.moveTo(pt.x, pt.y);
                else this.ctx.lineTo(pt.x, pt.y);
            }
            this.ctx.stroke();
        }

        // 2. Draw Nav2 Planned Global Path
        if (this.plannedPath.length > 1) {
            this.ctx.strokeStyle = "#38bdf8";
            this.ctx.lineWidth = 3;
            this.ctx.setLineDash([6, 4]); // Dashed glowing navigation line
            this.ctx.beginPath();
            for (let i = 0; i < this.plannedPath.length; i++) {
                const pt = this.transformer.worldToScreen(this.plannedPath[i].x, this.plannedPath[i].y);
                if (i === 0) this.ctx.moveTo(pt.x, pt.y);
                else this.ctx.lineTo(pt.x, pt.y);
            }
            this.ctx.stroke();
            this.ctx.setLineDash([]); // Reset dashed line
        }

        // 3. Draw Robot Chassis & Heading
        const center = this.transformer.worldToScreen(this.currentPose.x, this.currentPose.y);
        const pixelRadius = this.robotRadius * this.transformer.scale;

        this.ctx.save();
        this.ctx.translate(center.x, center.y);
        this.ctx.rotate(-this.currentPose.yaw); // Counter-clockwise to screen clockwise

        // Safety Inflation Buffer Ring
        this.ctx.strokeStyle = "rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.25)";
        this.ctx.lineWidth = 1;
        this.ctx.beginPath();
        this.ctx.arc(0, 0, pixelRadius + 12, 0, Math.PI * 2);
        this.ctx.stroke();

        // Main AMR Chassis Body
        this.ctx.fillStyle = "#0284c7"; // NavPro Blue
        this.ctx.strokeStyle = "#ffffff";
        this.ctx.lineWidth = 2.5;
        this.ctx.beginPath();
        this.ctx.arc(0, 0, pixelRadius, 0, Math.PI * 2);
        this.ctx.fill();
        this.ctx.stroke();

        // Orientation Heading Pointer (Points forward along +X)
        this.ctx.fillStyle = "#ffffff";
        this.ctx.beginPath();
        this.ctx.moveTo(pixelRadius * 0.4, -pixelRadius * 0.4);
        this.ctx.lineTo(pixelRadius * 1.1, 0); // Nose pointer
        this.ctx.lineTo(pixelRadius * 0.4, pixelRadius * 0.4);
        this.ctx.closePath();
        this.ctx.fill();

        this.ctx.restore();
    }
}

4. Hooking into the requestAnimationFrame Loop

To run the renderer at a silky smooth 60 FPS:

JAVASCRIPT
const transformer = new CoordinateTransformer(800, 600);
const entityRenderer = new DynamicEntityRenderer("dynamicCanvas", transformer);
const client = new NavProWebClient("localhost", 8080);

// Connect WebSocket telemetry to update internal pose
client.connectTelemetry((frame) => {
    entityRenderer.updateTelemetry(frame);
});

// Main 60 FPS Animation Loop
function animateLoop() {
    entityRenderer.render();
    requestAnimationFrame(animateLoop);
}

// Start rendering
requestAnimationFrame(animateLoop);

5. Summary & Next Steps

In this lesson, you built real-time dynamic rendering:

  • Implemented a 60 FPS render loop using requestAnimationFrame.
  • Visualized historical breadcrumbs, Nav2 paths, and metric robot footprints.
  • Decoupled $20\,\text{Hz}$ telemetry packet ingestion from $60\,\text{Hz}$ display rendering.

In Lesson 13, we will add interactive controls: Virtual On-Screen Touch Joysticks & Click-to-Navigate 2D Goals!
